newsitem.title: THAILAND: Plans to help Thai finance sector seen flawed.
newsitem.headline: Plans to help Thai finance sector seen flawed.

text.p: The Thai government's plans to bolster the finance sector are flawed and may underestimate the problems facing troubled firms, senior executives and consultants told a meeting of Thai financiers on Monday.

"Although at first glance, the (government) package seems practical in solving the systemic risk of financial institutions, there are some flaws," Banyong Pongpanich, executive director of major local broker Phatra Thanakit Plc wrote in a report accompanying a speech.

The government has pledged to support the finance sector and encourage consolidation among firms to decrease the risks of a financial collapse as the country faces its most severe economic crisis since the early 1980s.

Lenders have been hit by high exposure to a slumping local real estate market and a decline in economic growth to around six percent from near double digit expansion during the late 1980s and early 1990s.
Non-performing loans among finance companies were probably running at between 21.7 and 31.5 percent of total loans, Banyong said.

"As most financial institutions tend to continue lending to bad projects, especially if the projects are large, the government must give incentives to propel efficient resource reallocation," he said.
"With such large damage, outside resources seem necessary to recapitalise the finance industry."

With the government's strategy of encouraging consolidation in the finance sector dented by the collapse of a proposed merger between Finance One Plc and Thai Danu Bank Plc last month, executives said a revamp of merger rules was now urgently required to speed up consolidation.

"By allowing the process to be negotiated on a case by case basis there is no standard procedure for valuing finco (finance company) assets, thus making it difficult to minimize bailout costs," Banyong wrote.
But even successfully merged firms faced difficulties achieving the cost savings associated with similar consolidation in developed markets, the meeting was told.

"The cost reduction approach poses significant challenges in Thailand where we have some cultural issues surrounding staff redundancies ... there is no history of management dealing with these type of issues," Ronald Stride, managing partner of consultants Booz-Allen and Hamilton told the meeting.
Mergers typically produced cost savings of around 35 to 40 percent of which 70 to 80 percent came from reducing overheads including redundancies, Stride said.
If layoffs were unacceptable then merger candidates must adopt more flexible and imaginative approaches to staffing if substantial cost reductions are to be achieved.
But fragmentation in the sector, which contains around 90 firms, made flexibility difficult as succesful mergers required the consolidation of several small firms, Stride said.
"Achieving a level of critical mass by combining the smaller institutions is the issue that structurally faces the industry," he added.

"How to do that is a very critical question and has a large degree of pain associated with that unfortunately because you will have to merge not just one of two institutions but several institutions to achieve that," Stride said.
